questions.q: In the workflow file, why does every other job `need` the `build-and-test` job?
options: Because GitHub Actions requires alphabetical job ordering
So that a failing test stops every downstream job, including the image build and both deployments
It's purely decorative and has no functional effect
Because `needs` controls which runner operating system is used
questions.explain: The `needs:` keyword makes dependent jobs wait for build-and-test to succeed first — if tests fail, the image is never built and nothing deploys, enforcing Continuous Integration's core guarantee.

options: To make the job run faster
So the image is only built and pushed from the main branch, never from an untrusted pull request
Because YAML requires an `if` condition on every job
To disable the job entirely
questions.explain: This condition ensures the image build/push (and its registry credentials) only runs for code actually on main, not for arbitrary pull requests which could come from untrusted forks.

questions.q: What is the key functional difference between the `deploy-staging` and `deploy-production` jobs?
options: There is no difference — they behave identically
deploy-staging runs automatically; deploy-production waits for a human approval if the production environment has required reviewers configured
deploy-production runs before deploy-staging
deploy-staging requires a password but deploy-production does not
questions.explain: Staging is deployed via Continuous Deployment (fully automatic), while production uses Continuous Delivery — the environment's required reviewers setting pauses the job until a human approves it.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how does this same pipeline logic map to Azure Pipelines?
options: It cannot be done in Azure Pipelines at all
The same four stages map onto Azure Pipelines' stages block, using environments with approval checks for production — only the YAML dialect changes
Azure Pipelines does not support container builds
Azure Pipelines requires rewriting the application code
questions.explain: The same build/test, build-image, staging, and production stages map onto Azure Pipelines' own stage and environment constructs — the underlying logic is the same, just expressed in a different YAML dialect.

questions.q: What does the final 'before calling it done' checklist verify?
options: That the code has zero comments
That a broken test blocks the merge, a passing merge produces a tagged image, staging updates automatically, and production waits for approval
That the pipeline runs exactly once and never again
That the application uses a specific programming language
questions.explain: The checklist confirms the pipeline actually behaves as planned in Lesson 29: tests gate merges, images get built and tagged, staging deploys automatically, and production requires explicit approval.
